Often yes, especially at nurseries that specialize in native plants 🌱 One thing worth asking before you pay: whether the plants were treated with systemic insecticide. Treated leaves are lethal to caterpillars, and the plant looks perfectly healthy either way. A local native plant society usually knows exactly who sells clean stock.

A good year in your own yard is a real thing, so enjoy it 🦋 We would just be careful about reading a trend into one season, because the numbers swing hard from year to year. What the research keeps landing on is habitat: the loss of milkweed on the breeding grounds is the main driver of the long decline. More stems where you are is genuinely part of the answer, so whatever you did this year, keep doing it.

Fall is your friend in Sedona 🌾 Milkweed seed wants about a month of cold before it germinates reliably, and ours does not come pre-chilled, so a fall sowing lets the season do that work for you. The other route is a month in the fridge, then into pots. For hot and dry, narrowleaf and butterfly weed are the usual suspects. All eleven species we carry are North American natives and none of them is tropical milkweed, but an Arizona native plant list will be far more precise about your corner of the map than we can be from way up here.
Zones 3 through 9 covers everything we carry 🌿 And that number is a floor, not a ceiling: a species rated for zone 3 is perfectly content several zones warmer.

Three quarters of an acre for the critters, we love to hear it 🦋 Buying in person is the right instinct, and that is the one part we cannot help with, since we ship rather than sit on a shelf in Florida. What we can tell you is that none of the eleven species we carry is tropical milkweed; natives are the whole point here. For central Florida, your nearest native plant society chapter or a native plant nursery is the best door to knock on: they will know which growers keep clean stock and which species actually belong on your land.

Iguanas! That is a plot twist we never get up here 🦎 The usual story is that deer leave milkweed alone because the latex is so bitter, but clearly nobody forwarded that memo to your neighbours. If they keep helping themselves, a pot somewhere they cannot climb might be worth a shot 🌿

Four hanging in the enclosure and a fifth about to make the leap, that is a very good week 🦋 And harvesting your own swamp milkweed and butterfly weed seed on top of it, for a full reset. We are a little jealous of next spring at your place.
205 🦋 That stopped being a hobby a while ago. Thank you for every single one of them.

Two stripey ones in your photo, and then poof 🐛 We wish we had a clever trick to hand you, but a yard is a wild place and we are not about to invent one. What we can say is that the patch itself is the part you control, and the ones that do make it come from patches exactly like yours.
No caption needed 🌼 A butterfly settling into the marigolds, the barrel planter, the stone patio: that is a corner somebody clearly fusses over. Thanks for the view.

Fifty plants and one monarch is a rough ratio, and we feel that one 🌿 None of those stems are wasted though. A patch that size is a standing invitation, and it will be there whether or not they took you up on it this season.

Buffalo gives you good options 🌿 Common milkweed if you have room to let it roam, swamp milkweed if your spot stays damp, butterfly weed if you want something that behaves in a bed. All three belong in New York, and every species we carry is a North American native. A state native plant list will still nail your particular soil better than we can from up here.
Build it and they have a way of noticing 🦋 Your part is done, now it is on them to show up.
Seeds in hand before the season even asks for them, that is the good kind of impatient 🌱
That little squeal is the correct reaction 🦋 We felt it right through the screen.

Half a dozen caterpillars and a daughter proud enough to march you outside to see them 🐛 That is a very good yesterday.

Look at the size of that one 🐛 Plump, stripes glowing, and it has clearly been putting a dent in those leaves. Bonus points for the young pod forming further up the stem: your plant is running both jobs at once.
Ever growing is precisely what a milkweed patch is supposed to do 🌿 Give it a couple more seasons and you will be the one handing seed to the neighbours.

Worth saying out loud: a nectar plant and a host plant are two completely different jobs 🦋 The adults will drink from all sorts of things, but the caterpillars only ever eat milkweed. Room for both in a garden, though only one of them raises the next batch.
Spray does not stop politely at a property line, no. That is the maddening part of trying to keep one yard clean 🌿 Your own corner still counts for the ones passing through.
Tara, your friend is right and we are not about to pretend otherwise 🦋

That sad little face is fair enough 🥺 Even on a quiet monarch year those flowers are feeding a whole crowd of bees and beetles you are probably not counting, and the patch keeps its post for whenever the traffic picks back up.

A jar that smelled of dill is a wonderfully specific thing to carry around for decades 🐛 Childhood caterpillar projects stick with people far longer than anyone expects them to.
Already on it, we love to see it 🦋

Three feet tall means the hard part is behind you 🦋 And you do not need to buy anyone: the females do their own shopping, and a stand that size is exactly what they are scanning the neighbourhood for.
Monarchs everywhere like ants at a picnic, only magical. What a thing to have witnessed 🦋 Those Pacific Grove trips sound like the kind of memory that makes a person care for the rest of their life.
Watching it happen from your own yard lands very differently than reading about it somewhere 🌿 That is not a small thing to notice.
Clumps of butterfly weed and a caterpillar crowd to go with them, that is the whole thing working exactly as advertised 🧡

Two easy routes in the West Virginia valleys 🌱 Sow straight into the ground in the fall and let winter deliver the cold spell the seed needs, roughly a month of it, or keep them in the fridge for that month and start them in pots in spring. Ours are not pre-chilled, so one of the two has to happen. Then it is patience: leaves the first year, flowers the second.

Depends entirely which one you mean 🌿 Common milkweed is the big shouldery type that will happily fill a corner, while butterfly weed and swamp milkweed stay much more compact and behave themselves in a bed. Worth knowing the species before you choose the spot.

One a year with all that on offer is a genuinely puzzling result 🤷 Monarch traffic is uneven and none of us gets a vote in it. All anyone can do is be ready for the year they swing through, and you very clearly are.

Generally yes 🌿 The latex is bitter enough that browsing animals give milkweed a wide berth, which is why it often stands untouched in spots where everything else gets nibbled to the ground. No guarantee against a truly determined deer, mind you.

That is the classic pair of temperaments, honestly 🌿 Butterfly weed grows off a taproot and stays exactly where you put it, which is also why it takes its sweet time settling in, while the common one travels by rhizome and turns up three beds over. Worth knowing the caterpillars will happily take the common kind too, yours just have not found it yet, but if the orange has been doing all the work so far then by all means keep spreading it.
Friday evening to Saturday morning is frankly showing off 😄 They must have been circling the block waiting for you to finish planting.

It has that reputation and it is earned 🌱 The piece most people are missing is the cold: the seed wants roughly a month of it before it will germinate reliably, and ours does not arrive pre-chilled. Sow outdoors in the fall, or give them a month in the fridge first, and the odds change completely.
Dozens on a good day in a beach town is a lovely thing to be able to report 🦋 Enjoy every single one of them.

Clover in the mix, absolutely 🐝 Milkweed flowers pull in a serious bee crowd of their own, so the two get along very nicely in the same yard.

You can absolutely put more in now 🌱 If they are going in during the warm season, give them a month in the fridge first, since ours are not pre-chilled and that cold spell is what wakes them up. And do not write off the overwintered batch yet, milkweed is famously unhurried about surfacing.

Plenty of company turns up for the flowers 🐝 The blooms are seriously nectar-rich and pull in bees, butterflies and beetles of every description. For caterpillars it is a different story: milkweed is the monarch's plant specifically, the only one their larvae can use, which is exactly why the two are so bound together. So picture a nectar bar for the whole neighbourhood, with a nursery attached in case the monarchs ever swing your way.
Five different types at once, we admire the ambition 🌿 And an ugly fence is precisely the sort of place milkweed earns its keep. Hope they all take.
A magical part of your youth is about the best reason there is to get those seeds in the ground 🌱 It was everywhere once, and it can be again wherever you decide to put it.
Milkweed standing across CRP acres is the kind of scale that genuinely counts 🌿 A garden patch is lovely, but whole fields are how habitat actually comes back.
Finally is the operative word with this seed 🌱 Congratulations, the slow part is behind you now.

Bringing the Acadia page along, Rachel Carson passage and all, is a very good way to make a point 🦋 And you will get no argument from us: every species we carry is a straight native, nothing hybridized and nothing tropical.
Every single year, without fail 🌿 They seem to know exactly where the milkweed is before we do.

Fingers crossed over here too 🌱 Milkweed does enjoy keeping a person waiting before it commits to anything.
Good to hear it is holding its own down there 🌿 Wild stands quietly doing their thing are worth more than any bed the rest of us could plant on purpose.

Depends entirely on where you garden 🌿 Tell us your region and we can point you at the right one. The general split is simple enough in the meantime: room to roam means common milkweed, a tidy bed means butterfly weed, a damp corner means swamp milkweed.
Poke milkweed we do have 🌿 Asclepias exaltata, one of the eleven native species on our list. Good taste, too, it does not get asked for nearly as often as its cousins.

Iowa is spoiled for choice 🌿 Common milkweed and swamp milkweed are both thoroughly at home there, and butterfly weed as well if you want something that stays put. Every species we carry is a North American native, though an Iowa native plant list is always worth a glance before you commit.

Two of them working the onion blooms in your yard, not a milkweed in sight 🦋 That is the part people forget: the adults will drink from nearly anything, it is the caterpillars that are fussy. Lovely corner you have made back there.

Not at all, and it is a fair thing to ask 🌿 We carry eleven species and every one is a North American native, which is simply where our work sits. Eleven kinds of milkweed is a lot of milkweed, and which one belongs in your garden depends mostly on where you are.

Yes and yes 🌿 Showy milkweed is on our list and it is one of the better fits out your way. Still worth checking a native plant list for your specific corner, mind you, since California is roughly five climates in a trench coat.
Plucked off by hand and squeezed between finger and thumb, the old-fashioned method 🌿 Your plants sound like they are putting up a decent fight, and so are you.

What a gathering 🦋 They are all crowded onto the wet gravel at the water's edge rather than on any flower, which is a scene you really only get at a riverside. We will let someone with a field guide tell you exactly what they were after, but that is a lovely thing to have caught on camera.

A nursery actually named Asclepias, in Florida, full of monarchs 🦋 That is almost too on the nose. And pairing host plants with black-eyed susans for the nectar is exactly the right instinct: one feeds the caterpillars, the other feeds the grown-ups.

Solid advice, and it lines up with what we tell people 🌱 That cold spell is the whole trick. Ours do not arrive pre-chilled either, so it is winter outdoors or a stint in the fridge, one or the other.
Those filaments, front and back, waving around like the thing means business 🐛 A very well-fed one out for a stroll across the patio table. Thanks for the close-up.

Full sun is the one that really matters 🌞 Milkweed sulks in shade. Ground or pot both work fine: a pot is actually handy for the common kind since it keeps those wandering rhizomes in check, and butterfly weed does well in one thanks to its taproot. Whichever you choose, put a few together rather than one on its own, a clump is what gets noticed.

Zone 5 sits comfortably inside the range for everything we carry 🌿 The whole list is good from about 3 to 9, and that number marks the coldest a plant tolerates rather than a ceiling. For Wisconsin the obvious locals are common milkweed, swamp milkweed and butterfly weed, so it comes down to how much room you are willing to give them.

Good news, no 🌿 Milkweed is a perennial: it dies back over winter and comes up again on its own, usually a little stronger each year. The only patience it asks for is at the start, since a seed-grown plant tends to give you leaves the first year and flowers the second.

Full sun, honestly, and they will not thank you for shade 🌿 If the yard is mostly shaded, your best move is whatever sunny pocket you do have, even a small one. A tight bright corner beats a generous dark bed every time.
Prolific is exactly the word 🌸 Once milkweed decides it likes a spot, it does not do anything by halves.
That is the right order of operations 🌿 Region first, everything else after. A milkweed that belongs where you live will always do more good than one that simply looked nice in the pot.

Good idea for a post, noted 🌿 In the meantime, each of the eleven species has its own page with photos on lasclay.com. The differences are more obvious than people expect, butterfly weed especially, which is the bright orange one that never looks like any of the others.

A butterfly garden with almost nobody in it is a rough thing to stand in 🌿 We would rather not put a figure on a whole season from up here. What we can say is that the work you did is still done: the plants are in the ground, and that part does not undo itself.

Median strips and municipal edges add up to a startling amount of ground 🌿 If even a slice of it carried milkweed instead of mown grass, that is habitat at a scale no amount of private gardening can reach. Genuinely worth saying to a city councillor.

Free milkweed that shows up uninvited and brings monarchs along with it — that is the best kind of gardening there is 🦋 It travels by root and by seed, so once a patch decides it likes your yard, it tends to settle in for good. You did nothing and got everything.

That is exactly the right order of events 🌿 The butterflies turn up first, look the place over, and the caterpillars follow a little after. Have a peek at the undersides of the leaves in a few days — that is where the eggs like to hide.

Nectar and nursery, two different jobs 🦋 The butterfly bush feeds the grown-ups, but the caterpillars only eat milkweed — so the milkweed is the part that actually makes more monarchs. Lovely to have both on shift in the same yard.

Texas gives you a good hand to play 🌿 Several of the natives do well down that way — butterfly weed, swamp milkweed and green milkweed among them. The one we steer people away from is tropical milkweed. For the exact picks your county wants, a local native-plant society or nursery will know your ground far better than we can from up here.

Ah, that is a deflating result 🌿 Milkweed seed is stubborn on purpose: most of it wants about thirty days of cold and damp before it will wake up, which is why sowing in the fall works so much better than sowing in spring. And even when it does come up, year one is usually nothing but leaves — the flowers wait until year two. Worth giving that spot another look before writing it off.

A hundred and fifty years of being left alone is the rarest item on that list 🦋 Ground nobody has bothered keeps its milkweed without a single person planting a thing, and that is precisely the habitat the monarchs have been losing everywhere else. Sixty-four acres of it is genuine good news.
